Hard
hahrd
adj.
Old English heard, firm, severe, strong. Webster 1828: firm; solid; compact; not easily penetrated; difficult; oppressive; and, of the heart, unfeeling, obdurate. In the Authorized Version the word runs three ways — what is difficult, what is oppressive, and what is unyielding — and Scripture denies the first of God and asserts the third of man.

Biblical Definition

Scripture uses hard to draw a line between God and man, and the line runs the opposite way from what we expect. Of God, the question is asked and answered: Is any thing too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14). Jeremiah repeats it as a confession under siege: thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee (Jeremiah 32:17). Nothing is difficult to Him. But of man the word describes the heart, and there it is fatal. The warning stands over the whole letter to the Hebrews: Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:8). A hard heart is not a strong one; it is one that no longer registers what it hears. Proverbs adds the practical verdict on the life built that way: the way of transgressors is hard (Proverbs 13:15) — sin is not the easy road, whatever it advertises. And the unprofitable servant supplies the corruption in its own words, excusing his idleness by an accusation: I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown (Matthew 25:24). He calls the master hard, and the master’s reply exposes the hardness as the servant’s own. What a man believes about God’s hardness usually describes his heart, not God’s character.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HARD as firm; solid; compact; not easily penetrated or separated; difficult to understand or accomplish; laborious; oppressive; severe; and, of persons, unfeeling, insensible, obdurate.

expand to see more

HARD, a. [Sax. heard.] — Firm; solid; compact; not easily penetrated, or separated into parts; not soft. Difficult; not easy to the intellect. Laborious; fatiguing. Oppressive; rigorous; severe; as hard terms. Unfeeling; insensible; obdurate; as a hard heart.

Webster’s progression — from stone, to difficulty, to severity, to an unfeeling heart — is the biblical progression exactly. The last sense is a metaphor drawn from the first, and Ezekiel makes the figure explicit when God promises to take away the stony heart and give a heart of flesh.

Key Scripture

Genesis 18:14 — "Is any thing too hard for the LORD? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son."

Jeremiah 32:17 — "Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee:"

Hebrews 3:8 — "Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:"

Proverbs 13:15 — "Good understanding giveth favour: but the way of transgressors is hard."

Matthew 25:24 — "Then he which had received the one talent came and said, Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed:"

Modern Corruption

Hard is corrupted when the hardening of the heart is treated as something that merely happens to a man — a misfortune or a psychological injury — rather than an act for which Scripture holds him responsible and against which it issues a direct command.

expand to see more

Hebrews 3:8 is an imperative addressed to the will: Harden not your hearts. It is not a description of a condition that overtakes people. The modern instinct is to explain hardness as the residue of what a person has suffered, and therefore to treat it as an injury to be tended rather than a sin to be repented of. Scripture is more merciful than that, because it is more honest. It grants that hardening happens gradually, in a wilderness, through repeated provocation — and it still commands against it and still holds men accountable for it. Where hardness is only ever explained, it is never repented of, and a man may be sympathized with all the way to the judgment. The command implies that grace is available to obey it.

The second corruption is the servant’s in Matthew 25:24, and it is remarkably common: the sinner attributes hardness to God and uses that attribution to justify doing nothing. I knew thee that thou art an hard man is offered as an excuse and functions as an accusation. Scripture’s answer is that no such hardness exists in God toward His people — He is the God for whom nothing is too hard and who gave His own Son — and that the charge reveals the accuser. This matters wherever the doctrines of grace are taught, because sovereign election is regularly caricatured as making God hard. The Reformed answer is the servant’s parable read straight: the man who calls his master hard has not looked at the master, and the God who hardened Pharaoh is the same God who asked Abraham, with a son in view, whether anything is too hard for the LORD.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew keeps two distinct ideas apart that English merges. One root means too difficult, surpassing and is used of God’s ability; another means stiff, stubborn, severe and is used of man’s heart. The first is the same root that gives wonderful.

expand to see more

Hebrew pālā (H6381) — to be extraordinary, surpassing, beyond reach; the word behind too hard for the LORD (Genesis 18:14) and behind Wonderful in Isaiah 9:6.

Hebrew qāshāh (H7185) — to be hard, stiff, stubborn, severe; the verb of the hardened heart and the stiff neck.

Hebrew chāzaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen; also used of hardening, as of Pharaoh’s heart, where strengthening in resolve is the hardening.

Hebrew lēb (H3820) — heart; the organ of will and understanding, and therefore the thing that hardens. Not the seat of emotion merely, but of decision.

Usage

"Is any thing too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14) — the question is rhetorical, and Sarah heard it while laughing."

"Harden not your hearts (Hebrews 3:8) is an imperative, which means hardening is a thing men do rather than a thing that merely happens."

"The way of transgressors is hard (Proverbs 13:15): sin advertises ease and delivers difficulty."
